Volume 05 · Chapter 01

Preferences and consumer choice

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v02, v03, v04

By the endDerive demands and identify corner solutions under a budget constraint.

What a consumer chooses, and what the model assumes

Capability: derive demands and identify corner solutions under a budget constraint. Prerequisites: the mathematics, probability and empirical reasoning of Volumes 2–4, especially constrained optimization, continuity and compactness, and the distinction between a model and identified evidence. The foundation examination checks those tools. This chapter studies certain consumption bundles; it does not replace Volume 3's separate theory of utility over lotteries.

A household receives a fixed weekly spending allowance. It might split expenditure across two goods, buy only one, or accept several equally attractive combinations. A tangency diagram describes only some of those possibilities. We need to specify the alternatives and their ranking, define what is affordable, and then establish which bundles actually maximize that ranking.

Let x = (x₁,…,xₙ) be a bundle in X = ℝ+n. Each coordinate is a nonnegative quantity in its stated unit and period. A meal this week and a meal next month are different commodities if timing matters. Let p = (p₁,…,pₙ) be prices in USD per corresponding unit, and m be available spending in USD for the same decision. Thus p·x = Σpᵢxᵢ is expenditure in USD. Throughout the basic model, n is finite, goods are divisible, prices are linear and strictly positive, m ≥ 0, and the consumer takes prices as given. Saving, time costs, rationing and quality differences must be included if relevant; they are not silently resolved by the notation. All numerical preferences and observations below are synthetic teaching cases.

Preferences come before utility numbers

Write x ≽ y when x is at least as good as y for this consumer. Define strict preference x ≻ y by x ≽ y but not y ≽ x, and indifference x ∼ y by both weak comparisons. Completeness means every pair can be compared: x ≽ y or y ≽ x, possibly both. Transitivity means x ≽ y and y ≽ z imply x ≽ z. Together these are called rational preferences in this model. They describe coherent rankings, not moral worth, perfect information, selfishness or agreement with an observer's tastes.

A utility representation u: X → ℝ satisfies x ≽ y if and only if u(x) ≥ u(y). Numerical order is complete and transitive, so a represented preference has those properties. Conversely, on a finite set a complete transitive relation partitions alternatives into ordered indifference classes; assign increasing integers to those classes. This constructs a representation. On an infinite consumption set, completeness and transitivity alone do not guarantee the continuous representation needed for the existence arguments below. We will specify a utility function and its regularity instead of asserting that every possible ranking has the required representation.

For example, a lexicographic consumer first compares x₁ and uses x₂ only to break an exact tie. The rule is complete and transitive. Every (1/k,0) is preferred to (0,1), yet (1/k,0) converges to (0,0), which is worse than (0,1). No continuous utility representation can preserve those comparisons: continuity would make u(0,0) ≥ u(0,1) in the limit. This demonstrates a failed regularity condition; it is not a claim that the consumer cannot rank the bundles.

If f is strictly increasing on the range of u, then f(u(x)) ≥ f(u(y)) exactly when u(x) ≥ u(y). Therefore f∘u represents the same preferences and gives the same maximizing bundles. A merely nondecreasing transformation may merge previously distinct ranks; a decreasing transformation reverses them. Utility here is ordinal: a level of 20 versus 10 is not evidence of twice as much satisfaction, and differences are not automatically comparable across people.

Marginal utility is representation-dependent. If u(x) = x₁ + x₂, its first marginal utility is 1. The equivalent representation (x₁ + x₂)³ has first marginal utility 3(x₁ + x₂)², which increases with x₁. Nothing about the consumer's ranking changed. Thus diminishing marginal utility is a feature of a chosen representation, not a general implication of rational preferences. For expected utility over lotteries, applying a nonlinear transformation inside an expectation can change rankings: Volume 3's positive-affine restriction remains relevant there.

Wolitzky's MIT choice and preference slides, particularly slides 7–16 and 20–27, distinguish rationality, ordinal representation and additional regularity assumptions. The definitions and examples here make those assumptions explicit rather than deriving them from a claim that all consumers behave alike.

Continuity, convexity and nonsatiation do different jobs

For a continuous preference relation, if xk → x and yk → y with xk ≽ yk for every k, then x ≽ y. A continuous utility representation ensures this property by passing its weak inequalities to limits. It rules out the lexicographic limiting reversal above. Continuity will also let a utility maximum be attained on a compact budget set.

The upper contour set at z is {x ∈ X: x ≽ z}. Preferences are convex when each such set is convex: if x and y are each at least as good as z, any mixture θx + (1 − θ)y, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, is also at least as good as z. For this divisible-goods model, a mixture is an ordinary average bundle, not a lottery. Preferences are strictly convex if, for distinct such x and y and 0 < θ < 1, the mixture is strictly better than z.

In utility language, convex preferences mean quasiconcavity:

u(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≥ min{u(x),u(y)}.

To see the equivalence, take the lower-ranked endpoint as the reference bundle z; conversely, if both endpoints have utility at least u(z), the displayed minimum also does. Strict quasiconcavity replaces ≥ with > for distinct endpoints and interior mixtures. Concavity of u is sufficient for quasiconcavity because a weighted average of two values is at least their minimum. It is not necessary: (x₁ + x₂)³ represents convex preferences but is not a concave utility function on ℝ+². Strictly increasing transformations preserve the ranking and its convexity, even when they change the utility function's curvature.

Local nonsatiation means that for every x ∈ X and every ε > 0, some y ∈ X with ‖y − x‖ < ε satisfies y ≻ x. There is a preferred bundle arbitrarily close, with the neighborhood interpreted relative to X, including its boundary. Strict monotonicity—raising at least one good without reducing another makes a bundle strictly better—implies local nonsatiation here. Weak monotonicity alone does not: constant utility is weakly increasing and locally satiated everywhere. Local nonsatiation itself does not say that every good is desirable. These are separate restrictions, and a bliss point can make budget exhaustion fail.

The budget and the demand correspondence

The feasible budget set and Marshallian demand are

B(p,m) = {x ∈ ℝ+n: p·x ≤ m},
D(p,m) = arg maxx∈B(p,m) u(x).

The notation arg max denotes the set of maximizing bundles, not the largest utility value. A correspondence can return several bundles. Only when that set contains exactly one bundle will we write a demand function x(p,m). “Marshallian” means that prices and money income are the inputs to this choice problem. It does not mean every good's demand must fall when its price rises.

Existence, and why positive prices matter

For pᵢ > 0 and finite m ≥ 0, B is nonempty because it contains zero. Its inequalities define a closed set, and 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ m/pᵢ bounds every coordinate. Thus B is compact in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. A continuous u attains a maximum there, so D is nonempty. When m = 0, B = {0} and demand is uniquely zero, regardless of the ranking. Negative m would make this nonnegative-consumption budget empty.

If a price is zero, the boundedness argument disappears. With p = (0,1), m = 1 and u = x₁ + x₂, increasing free x₁ makes utility unbounded; no maximum exists. This shows a failure possibility, not that every zero-price problem lacks an optimum. Additional satiation or quantity constraints can change it. Similarly, discontinuous utility on a compact budget need not attain its supremum.

Three properties with short proofs

Budget exhaustion under local nonsatiation. Suppose an optimum x leaves slack s = m − p·x > 0. Choose a neighborhood radius ε < s/‖p‖. Every nonnegative y within that radius satisfies p·y ≤ p·x + ‖p‖‖y − x‖ < m. Local nonsatiation supplies a preferred y there, contradicting optimality. Hence every optimum spends p·x = m. The statement concerns the specified goods: leaving cash unspent may simply mean that cash or future consumption was omitted from the model.

Homogeneity of degree zero. For any t > 0, (tp)·x ≤ tm is equivalent to p·x ≤ m. The feasible set and ranking are identical, so D(tp,tm) = D(p,m). This is a simultaneous nominal rescaling with unchanged preferences and commodity definitions. Raising income alone is a different experiment.

Convex demand sets and uniqueness. If preferences are convex, two maximizers have equally high rank; any feasible mixture is at least as good, hence also maximizes. Therefore D is convex. With strict convexity, a mixture of two distinct maximizers would be strictly better, a contradiction: at most one maximizer exists. Combine this with existence to obtain a unique demand. Strict convexity is sufficient, not necessary; a kinked example below has unique demand despite lacking strict convexity. These arguments require a convex feasible set. An integer restriction can break it.

MIT's consumer theory slides, slides 2–10 and 19–21, supply the corresponding budget, demand and multiplier framework. Here money income is m; the source uses w.

Indifference curves and the limits of tangency

In two goods, an indifference curve is a set of bundles with the same utility. Distinct indifference classes cannot cross: a common bundle would make their ranks identical by transitivity. Curves need not always slope downward. Where u is differentiable and u₂ ≠ 0, holding utility fixed gives

u₁ dx₁ + u₂ dx₂ = 0,   dx₂/dx₁ = −u₁/u₂.

We define the marginal rate of substitution MRS₁₂ = u₁/u₂, the amount of good 2 the consumer locally gives up for one extra unit of good 1 along that curve when both marginal utilities are positive. The curve's slope is its negative. MRS has units of good 2 per unit of good 1. Under a differentiable transformation f∘u with f′(u) > 0, both marginal utilities acquire the same positive factor, so MRS is unchanged. If that derivative is zero, the transformed derivative ratio may be 0/0 even though the ranking and geometric curve remain unchanged.

The budget boundary is x₂ = m/p₂ − (p₁/p₂)x₁, with intercepts m/p₁ and m/p₂ and slope −p₁/p₂. At a smooth interior optimum with both goods consumed, a binding budget and positive marginal utilities, the two slopes coincide. Otherwise a small budget-preserving transfer toward the good with greater marginal utility per dollar would raise utility. This is a necessary local condition under the stated assumptions, not an all-purpose solution formula.

For differentiable u and m > 0, write the maximization Lagrangian as ℒ = u(x) + λ(m − p·x) + Σμᵢxᵢ. With λ ≥ 0, μᵢ ≥ 0, feasibility and complementary slackness, stationarity gives

uᵢ − λpᵢ + μᵢ = 0;
uᵢ/pᵢ = λ if xᵢ > 0;   uᵢ/pᵢ ≤ λ if xᵢ = 0.

At an optimum under local nonsatiation the budget binds and some coordinate is positive. The positive-price budget gradient and the gradients of zero-coordinate constraints are linearly independent: a linear combination can vanish in a positive coordinate only if the budget coefficient is zero, after which all other coefficients vanish. Thus the earlier KKT necessity condition applies when u is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of the point. At a nondifferentiable kink use direct feasible comparisons instead; at m = 0 use the singleton budget directly.

When the chosen representation is concave, a feasible KKT point is globally optimal. For any feasible z, the tangent inequality gives u(z) ≤ u(x) + ∇u(x)·(z − x). The last inner product is λp·(z − x) − μ·(z − x) ≤ 0 by feasibility and complementary slackness. This proves sufficiency. Without such a global argument, checking tangency alone can leave a minimum or another nonmaximizing stationary point. Also, λ is measured in the chosen utility scale per USD, so it changes when the utility representation is rescaled.

Worked example 1: an interior demand with ordinal curvature

Let u(x₁,x₂) = x₁²x₂ on ℝ+², with p₁,p₂ > 0 and m > 0. Coordinates are numerical quantities in fixed units. The function is continuous, so a maximizer exists. Any zero-coordinate bundle has utility zero; spending a positive amount on each good achieves positive utility. Thus an optimum is interior. It also exhausts the budget: at positive quantities, increasing either good raises utility.

On that positive domain, maximizing u is equivalent to maximizing log u = 2 log x₁ + log x₂. Logs apply to quantities normalized by the fixed reference units. This representation has Hessian diag(−2/x₁², −1/x₂²), negative definite. Its conditions are 2/x₁ = λp₁ and 1/x₂ = λp₂. Multiplying by quantities and summing gives 3 = λm, so

x₁(p,m) = 2m/(3p₁),   x₂(p,m) = m/(3p₂).

These positive quantities are feasible and satisfy the conditions. Strict concavity of the logarithmic objective proves they are the unique optimum among positive bundles; zero-coordinate bundles were already excluded. This proof does not assume that the original cubic utility is concave or that its boundary indifference sets are strictly convex everywhere.

At p = (4,6) USD per unit and m = 90 USD per week, demand is (15,5) units per week. Expenditures are 60 and 30 USD. In the original representation, MRS₁₂ = 2x₂/x₁ = 2/3, equal to p₁/p₂. The consumer spends two-thirds of this budget on good 1, a consequence of this functional form. Raising p₁ to 5 while holding m and p₂ fixed gives (12,5). Doubling both prices and income to (8,12;180) leaves (15,5). These are different comparative experiments; neither formula asserts that all real households have constant expenditure shares.

Worked example 2: the same smooth preference can produce two kinds of corner

Let u(x₁,x₂) = a log(1 + x₁) + x₂, with a > 0 and nonnegative, normalized quantities. The second good's marginal utility is 1, so the preference is locally nonsatiated. For p₁,p₂ > 0 and m ≥ 0, substitute budget exhaustion x₂ = (m − p₁x₁)/p₂. On 0 ≤ x₁ ≤ m/p₁ the resulting derivative and curvature are

g′(x₁) = a/(1 + x₁) − p₁/p₂,   g″(x₁) = −a/(1 + x₁)² < 0.

The unique maximizing first quantity is the stationary candidate restricted to its feasible interval:

x₁(p,m) = min{m/p₁, max{0, ap₂/p₁ − 1}},
x₂(p,m) = [m − p₁x₁(p,m)]/p₂.

To justify the formula, if g′ is already nonpositive at zero, the strictly concave objective declines from its left endpoint. If the zero of g′ lies inside, it gives the unique peak. If that zero exceeds m/p₁, the objective is increasing throughout the feasible interval and the right endpoint wins. At equality with an endpoint, that endpoint is still unique; m = 0 gives the sole feasible zero bundle. No negative quantity is allowed to survive as a supposed solution.

Take a = 9 and p = (3,1). At m = 18, the stationary x₁ = 2 is feasible, yielding (2,12). At m = 3, the budget permits at most x₁ = 1, so demand is (1,0). At this right corner MRS = 9/2 = 4.5, exceeding the price ratio 3. More good 1 would require negative good 2, so tangency is unavailable. The consumed good has u₁/p₁ = 1.5, while the absent good has u₂/p₂ = 1 ≤ 1.5, as required.

Now set p = (12,1) and m = 18. The stationary candidate is −1/4 and must be rejected; demand is (0,18). At this left corner u₁/p₁ = 9/12 ≤ u₂/p₂ = 1. A smooth utility does not guarantee an interior choice. If a separate ration limits x₁, that limit must also be included in its feasible interval and may create another binding boundary.

Worked example 3: ties and a kink are different reasons to avoid tangency

For perfect substitutes u = 3x₁ + 2x₂, compare utility gained per dollar: 3/p₁ and 2/p₂. If one is strictly larger, spend everything on that good; every dollar transferred to the other lowers utility. At p = (3,2) and m = 24 the ratios tie at 1. Utility equals expenditure, so every bundle on 3x₁ + 2x₂ = 24 maximizes. Demand is the entire segment from (8,0) to (0,12), not its midpoint alone. At p = (4,2), the second good gives more utility per dollar, so unique demand becomes (0,12).

For a different consumer, u = min{x₁,2x₂}. To attain utility t ≥ 0 requires x₁ ≥ t and x₂ ≥ t/2. At the same p = (3,2), these lower bounds cost at least 3t + 2(t/2) = 4t. With m = 24, t ≤ 6; the bundle (6,3) attains that upper bound. Positive prices force both component bounds to be equalities at utility 6, proving uniqueness. The indifference curve has a kink there, so a single derivative-based MRS is unavailable.

This fixed-proportions preference is convex and locally nonsatiated: increasing both goods improves it, though adding only the already abundant component may not. It is not strictly convex: distinct bundles on a flat portion of one indifference curve can have an indifferent mixture. Its unique demand demonstrates that strict convexity is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. More generally, for u = min{x₁/a,x₂/b}, a,b > 0, utility t needs a units of good 1 and b of good 2 per unit of t. The unique positive-price optimum is t = m/(ap₁ + bp₂), x = (at,bt), including x = 0 when m = 0.

Revealed preference: what observed affordability can rule out

Suppose the same consumer faces observed budgets Bt and makes optimizing choices with a stable ranking. If xt is chosen while xs is affordable, then xt ≽ xs. This is a directly revealed weak preference. Nonselection by itself need not mean strict inferiority: the observer may have recorded only one of several tied maximizers.

WARP when the complete choice correspondence is known

Let C(B) record all maximizing bundles in each budget, rather than one arbitrary selection. The weak axiom of revealed preference (WARP) requires: if x and y are available in both B and B′, x ∈ C(B), and y ∈ C(B′), then x ∈ C(B′). A fixed complete transitive ranking implies this rule. The first choice gives x ≽ y; the second gives y at least as good as every bundle in B′. Transitivity makes x at least as good as every such bundle too, so x must belong to C(B′). A violation is incompatible with that claimed complete choice correspondence.

When demand is unique, C(B) = {x} and C(B′) = {y} with x ≠ y, mutual affordability is therefore impossible. With budget exhaustion, the familiar single-valued budget version is

xt ≠ xs and pt·xs ≤ pt·xt
imply ps·xt > ps·xs.

The strict conclusion uses uniqueness, or an equivalent restriction on the complete choice rule. It cannot be imposed on a record containing one possibly tied choice per budget without addressing ties.

A necessary pairwise budget test that permits ties

For possibly tied choices generated by utility maximization with local nonsatiation, the necessary implication is weaker:

pt·xs ≤ pt·xt
implies ps·xt ≥ ps·xs.

This is often called the tie-permitting or weak budget form of WARP; terminology varies, so use the displayed inequalities. To prove it, the first comparison gives u(xt) ≥ u(xs). If the reverse affordability were strict, xt would lie strictly inside budget s. Local nonsatiation then gives a nearby affordable z with u(z) > u(xt), contradicting the optimality of xs. Thus no weak revealed comparison may be reversed by a strict affordability comparison. Check all ordered pairs, so a strict inequality on either side is detected. Equalities in both directions can be consistent with genuine indifference.

For example, at identical prices (1,1) and income 5, observing (4,1) once and (1,4) another time is consistent with u = x₁ + x₂ and arbitrary selection among tied maximizers. It does not come from a unique-demand model. The full maximizing correspondence on that budget is the same segment on both occasions; recording one endpoint is not evidence that the other was excluded from it.

Bergstrom's Notes on Revealed Preference, pages 1–3, explicitly distinguishes the conventional no-reversal rule from the treatment of ties and longer revealed-preference chains. The complete-correspondence convention is also set out in MIT's choice slides. We use the inequalities above to avoid importing an unstated uniqueness assumption.

Pairwise consistency is a limited test

A chain of affordable-choice comparisons gives a chain of weak utility inequalities. It cannot end with a strict reversal. Pairwise checks alone can miss a cycle across three or more observations; Exercise 8 constructs one. We use this necessary chain restriction without claiming to prove a general finite-data rationalization theorem here.

A failed test rejects a joint account: stable preferences, correct commodity definitions and prices, complete feasible budgets, optimizing choice and any stated nonsatiation or uniqueness assumptions. Unrecorded coupons, changed product quality, household composition, a quantity limit or measurement error can change that account. Passing a finite test does not identify a unique utility function, prove stable preferences outside the observations, establish a causal price effect or license interpersonal welfare comparisons. The economic content lies in both the restrictions and the reasons their maintained assumptions are credible.

Exercises

  1. Audit an ordinal claim. On ℝ+², let u = x₁ + x₂. Decide which of u³, −u and (u − 5)² represent the same preference on the entire domain. Use bundles (2,1) and (1,3) where useful. Compare u₁ with the first marginal utility of u³, and explain why their difference does not change the consumer's preferences. Would replacing a Bernoulli utility inside an expected-utility calculation by its cube be justified by this argument alone?
  2. Identify the hypothesis doing the work. Let p = (3,2), m = 12 and u = −(x₁ − 1)² − (x₂ − 2)². Find demand and unspent income; identify why budget exhaustion need not hold. Prove homogeneity D(tp,tm) = D(p,m) directly for any t > 0. Explain what happens at m = 0 for positive prices, and why p = (0,2), m = 12, u = x₁ + x₂ need not have a maximizing bundle.
  3. Derive a new smooth demand. For u = x₁³x₂², p₁,p₂ > 0 and m > 0, derive demand rather than importing Worked example 1's shares. Justify interiority and global uniqueness. Calculate demand, expenditure shares and MRS at p = (2,5), m = 50. Then halve p₁ alone, and separately double all prices and income. Distinguish the two experiments.
  4. Use boundary derivatives. For u = 6 log(1 + x₁) + x₂, find demand at (p₁,p₂,m) = (2,1,3), (2,1,10) and (7,1,10). Check the relevant marginal-utility-per-dollar equality or inequality in each case. At (2,1,10), impose an additional ration x₁ ≤ 1; solve again and explain why tangency to the ordinary budget line is no longer required.
  5. Demand can be a set. Let u = 2x₁ + 3x₂, p = (2,3) and m = 18. Describe the full demand correspondence, then change p₁ to 3 and solve. Under the original prices, list all maximizing bundles if both goods must be nonnegative integers. Separately, for u = √x₁ + √x₂, p = (1,1), m = 1, compare the divisible-goods optimum with the integer-good optima. Which premise of the strict-convexity uniqueness proof is lost?
  6. A kink with a unique answer. A consumption kit uses two units of good 1 and three of good 2, represented by u = min{x₁/2,x₂/3}. For p = (3,1), m = 24, derive the unique demand using a bound on affordable utility. Redo it when p₁ doubles. Explain why a derivative-based tangency is unnecessary, why local nonsatiation holds, and why uniqueness here does not establish strict convexity of the preference.
  7. A revealed-preference contradiction, or a tie? A consumer with stable locally nonsatiated preferences chooses xA = (4,1) at pA = (2,1), mA = 9, and xB = (1,4) at pB = (1,2), mB = 9. Compute all four own/cross expenditures and apply the tie-permitting pairwise test. Show the utility contradiction. Contrast with the same two choices at the identical budget p = (1,1), m = 5. State two pieces of information needed before interpreting an empirical violation as evidence against stable optimizing behavior.
  8. Why pairs are not enough. In three goods, observe choices xA = (1,0,0), xB = (0,1,0), xC = (0,0,1), all at income 3, with respective price vectors (3,2,4), (4,3,2) and (2,4,3). Form the expenditure matrix whose row t prices every chosen bundle at pt. Check the pairwise unique-demand WARP inequalities. Then prove that no stable locally nonsatiated utility maximization model can generate all three choices. Explain the scope of this falsification without claiming that pairwise success proves rationalizability.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Since u ≥ 0, cubing is strictly increasing on its range and preserves every ranking. Negation reverses strict ranks. Squaring u − 5 is not increasing over the full range: the two bundles have u values 3 and 4, but transformed values 4 and 1, reversing their order. Originally u₁ = 1, while ∂(u³)/∂x₁ = 3(x₁ + x₂)². Different marginal numbers do not imply different indifference sets or choices. Where x₁ + x₂ > 0, the ratio of the transformed marginal utilities remains 1; at the origin both are zero and the derivative ratio alone is uninformative. The certain-bundle ordinal argument does not authorize cubing Bernoulli utility inside an expectation. For example, a certain utility of 6/5 beats an equal-chance lottery over utilities 0 and 2 in expected utility, since 6/5 > 1. Cubing the Bernoulli numbers reverses the comparison: 216/125 < (0 + 8)/2 = 4. Expected-utility representations preserve lottery rankings under positive affine transformations, not arbitrary strictly increasing ones.
  2. The utility is at most zero and attains zero only at (1,2). That bundle costs 3 + 4 = 7 ≤ 12, so it is the unique optimum and leaves 5 USD. It is a bliss point: there is no strictly better nearby bundle, so local nonsatiation fails. This is compatible with continuity and strict concavity. For any t > 0, tp·x ≤ tm if and only if p·x ≤ m; the sets and objective agree, proving identical demand correspondences even in this satiated case. Positive prices with m = 0 allow only zero. With p = (0,2) and utility x₁ + x₂, any affordable bundle can be improved by adding free good 1, so no maximizer exists; its utility is unbounded above.
  3. Continuity on the compact budget gives existence. Axis bundles have utility zero, while some positive bundle is feasible and has positive utility, so every optimum is interior. There maximize 3 log x₁ + 2 log x₂; its negative definite diagonal Hessian gives strict concavity. Conditions 3/x₁ = λp₁ and 2/x₂ = λp₂ imply λm = 5, yielding x₁ = 3m/(5p₁) and x₂ = 2m/(5p₂). These satisfy feasibility and are the unique positive maximizer, hence the unique global one. At (2,5;50), demand is (15,4), expenditures (30,20), and shares (3/5,2/5). MRS = 3x₂/(2x₁) = 12/30 = 2/5 = p₁/p₂. Halving only p₁ gives (30,4). Doubling both prices and income to (4,10;100) preserves (15,4). The first changes a relative price at fixed money income; the second preserves the entire feasible budget.
  4. The unrestricted stationary x₁ is 6p₂/p₁ − 1. At (2,1,3) it equals 2 but affordability caps x₁ at 3/2, giving (3/2,0). Here u₁ = 6/(5/2) = 12/5, so u₁/p₁ = 6/5 ≥ u₂/p₂ = 1. At (2,1,10), demand is (2,6), with both marginal utilities per dollar equal to 1. At (7,1,10), the stationary candidate is −1/7, so demand is (0,10); the absent good has u₁/p₁ = 6/7 ≤ 1. With the additional ration at (2,1,10), maximize over 0 ≤ x₁ ≤ 1. The budget-substituted derivative is 6/(1+x₁) − 2, positive through this interval; demand is (1,8). At that point MRS = 3 > p₁/p₂ = 2. More good 1 would raise utility if the ordinary budget were the only restriction, but violates the ration. The extra constraint supplies the relevant boundary.
  5. At the original prices, utility equals expenditure, so D is {x ≥ 0: 2x₁ + 3x₂ = 18}, with endpoints (9,0) and (0,6). After p₁ becomes 3, utility per dollar is 2/3 for good 1 versus 1 for good 2, so D = {(0,6)}. With integer goods at the original prices, equality is attainable and necessary for maximum utility 18. The nonnegative integer solutions are (9,0), (6,2), (3,4) and (0,6). For the square-root utility on the unit continuous budget, budget exhaustion gives x₂ = 1 − x₁; symmetry and strict concavity give unique optimum (1/2,1/2), utility √2. With integer goods, the only feasible bundles are (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1), and the last two tie at utility 1. The integer feasible set is not convex: the preferred midpoint of the two optima is unavailable. Strictly convex preferences alone cannot restore that missing feasibility premise.
  6. Utility t requires x₁ ≥ 2t and x₂ ≥ 3t, costing at least (2p₁ + 3p₂)t. At (3,1;24), 9t ≤ 24, so t ≤ 8/3; the bundle (16/3,8) attains it and spends 16 + 8 = 24. Because prices are positive and the lower component bounds already exhaust the budget at that utility, any excess of either component would be unaffordable, proving uniqueness. At p = (6,1), t = 24/15 = 8/5 and demand is (16/5,24/5), with expenditure 96/5 + 24/5 = 24. Both optima occur at a kink; no differentiable MRS equality is needed. Increasing both quantities slightly raises their minimum, giving local nonsatiation, while an increase in an already abundant component may not improve utility. Along a flat part of an indifference curve, a mixture of distinct indifferent bundles can remain indifferent; strict convexity fails despite unique positive-price demand.
  7. The expenditure matrix in A/B row and column order is [[9,6],[6,9]]. Each chosen bundle costs the full income, and each alternative chosen elsewhere is strictly cheaper. At A, B is strictly inside the budget. Local nonsatiation provides a feasible bundle better than B, so optimal A must satisfy u(A) > u(B). At B the reverse reasoning gives u(B) > u(A), a contradiction. This fails even the tie-permitting test. At identical prices (1,1), both bundles cost 5. The linear utility x₁ + x₂ makes all full-budget bundles tied, so selecting either is consistent with optimization. It is inconsistent only with the additional claim of unique demand at that budget, not with arbitrary tied selections. Empirical checks must establish, for example, unchanged commodity quality/household preferences and the complete effective prices and constraints, including coupons, rations and outside options. Alternative missing-information examples earn credit if they explain how affordability or the comparison changes.
  8. The matrix is [[3,2,4],[4,3,2],[2,4,3]]. A reveals preference over B; at B's prices A costs 4 > 3. B reveals preference over C; at C's prices B costs 4 > 3. C reveals preference over A; at A's prices C costs 4 > 3. The other directed antecedents are false, so every distinct ordered pair passes the unique-demand WARP implication. Nevertheless, each of the three affordable alternatives costs only 2 when the chosen bundle costs 3. The local-nonsatiation/slack argument gives u(A) > u(B), u(B) > u(C) and u(C) > u(A), impossible for a real-valued utility or a transitive strict ranking. Thus pairwise checks can miss a longer cycle. The observation rejects the specified stable locally nonsatiated maximizing account with these complete budgets; it does not identify whether real-data failure would arise from preference change, measurement, omitted constraints or nonoptimizing choice.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain why ordinal utility can change its marginal numbers without changing choice; prove budget exhaustion and identify exactly where local nonsatiation enters; then use one interior, one corner and one tied demand to explain why “equate MRS to the price ratio” is incomplete. Distinguish an observed choice from a complete choice correspondence before interpreting WARP.

Delayed check: after several days, solve u = 4 log(1 + x₁) + x₂ at p = (2,1), first with m = 8 and then m = 1. Verify the boundary conditions and explain simultaneous price-income doubling. Answers: (1,6) with MRS = 2 in the first case; (1/2,0) with u₁/p₁ = 4/3 ≥ 1 in the second; simultaneous doubling leaves both feasible sets and choices unchanged. Finally explain why two different choices on one unchanged budget may represent a tie, while a strict affordability cycle under local nonsatiation cannot.

The next chapter, demand, duality and welfare, asks how much expenditure is needed to attain a specified preference level and how price responses combine substitution and income effects. Keep the present distinction between a correspondence, a unique demand and a differentiable demand: each additional conclusion requires its own conditions.

Sources and further study

  • Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lectures 1–2, Choice, Preference, and Utility (2015) — Method reference for complete/transitive preferences, ordinal representations, continuity, monotonicity/local nonsatiation, convex/strictly convex preferences and quasiconcavity; complete-choice-correspondence WARP convention.
  • Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lectures 3–4, Consumer Theory (2015) — Method reference for the positive-price linear budget, Marshallian demand correspondence, compact-budget existence, degree-zero homogeneity, LNS budget exhaustion and interior/corner KKT inequalities.
  • Ted Bergstrom, UCSB Economics 210A: Notes on Revealed Preference (17 November 2016) — Author-hosted primary notes on conventional budget WARP, the problem of tied choices, strict affordability under local nonsatiation and longer revealed-preference chains.
